lignes.texte: By the end of World War II, the most advanced air force on Earth was reduced to using teams of oxen
to tow Me-262 jet fighters to the runway. People often imagine the Nazi regime as the
pinnacle of industrial efficiency. But behind the propaganda was a system crippled by bureaucracy,
chronic shortages, and desperate decisions. Germany had world-class engineers, yet Hitler
repeatedly overruled his own experts as fuel, transport, and supplies ran out.
Germany looked unstoppable… until the Allies exposed its fatal weaknesses.
In October 1944, Adolf Hitler’s Minister of Armaments and War Production, Albert Speer,
visited a airfield near the Po River in Italy. He could barely believe what he was seeing. Some
of Germany’s most advanced planes were being pulled down the runway by cows and horses.
The problem was oil. Or the lack of it.
Speer later wrote he saw a colon of 150 trucks, with 4 oxen hitched to each one.
It was clear evidence of how an oil shortage was losing Germany the war.
On the Western Front, German army groups were being obliterated by Allied attacks because they
didn’t have enough fuel to move. In the east, the situation was even worse. The Red Army had
shattered Army Group Centre and was driving the surviving German forces back toward the Reich.
One of the main reasons was the Allied Oil Campaign.
Month after month, thousands of Allied bombers pounded Germany's synthetic fuel plants.
Tens of thousands of tons of bombs were dropped, starving the Reich of the fuel it
needed to fight. Things became so desperate that in November, the order came down -- “Anyone using
fuel for purposes other than the immediate conduct of operations will be considered a
saboteur and court-martialed without mercy.” During this time, production levels were
floundering at about 21% of their regular output. Future historians would call it a
gradual but “fatal decline.” The once-formidable Germany war machine had been rendered a hopeless
cripple. The Reich’s weapons continued to fly off assembly lines, but the finished products,
the machines that had once gripped the whole of Europe in fear, were sitting idle.
One of the most advanced aircraft of the war — the Messerschmitt Me 262,
the world's first operational jet fighter — was being dragged around a German
airfield by a farm animal. Hitler would be seething.
For a regime that prided itself on its technological prowess, the optics were ugly.
Germany, the self-proclaimed superpower of the future, looked as though it
had slipped back into the Dark Ages. In October that year, the Germans built
around 1,400 ME 262s and placed them operation squadrons but with such severe fuel shortages,
the pilots were badly trained. More aircraft were lost in accidents than were shot down in combat.
It took 5 years of war for the Allies to figure out Germany’s pressure point. They
severely underestimated how dependent Germany had become on its oil plants.
Flying ace General Adolf Galland later admitted: “The most successful operation…
was against the German fuel supply. This was… the fatal blow for the Luftwaffe!”
Galland could never understand why the Allies had not concentrated on it sooner. The fuel shortage,
he said, was “unbearable.” The Luftwaffe was the first branch of the German military
to be crippled by it. The rest would follow.
But something else was wrecking Germany’s war effort and it was
far from the burning oil plants at home. By 1944, around 90% of Germany's aviation
fuel and more than half of its total petroleum products came from synthetic fuel plants. It
was those plants that Allied bombers had been dropping bombs on. Prior to the devastating raids,
the plants had produced around 5 to 6 million tons of fuel each year. Without them, Germany could
never have waged war on the scale that it did. It didn't have much natural petroleum
but what it did have was… coal. Unlike Britain, the US and the Soviet Union,
which all had access to large domestic oil fields or reliable overseas supplies,
Germany’s coal was pivotal to its war effort. It was coal that could be transformed into
synthetic liquid fuel. Companies such as IG Farben converted it into gasoline, diesel,
lubricants and aviation fuel. The technology had been developed before Hitler came to power,
but after 1933 his government invested heavily in expanding it as part of its
drive towards economic self-sufficiency. For Hitler, this was his ticket to expansion.
He was planning to head out East. Beyond the borders of Poland lay the vast natural
resources of the Soviet Union: grain from Ukraine, massive coal reserves, iron ore and the oil fields
of the Caucasus. Germany's synthetic fuel industry could sustain rearmament, but it could never fully
meet the demands of a huge global conflict. So, to become economically self-sufficient,
Germany had to conquer resource-rich territory. Hitler first annexed Austria and occupied
Czechoslovakia, which brought valuable industry, raw materials and manpower.
Poland would bring more, but that eventually triggered war with Britain and France.
General Georg Thomas, responsible for Germany's war economy, estimated that such a conflict would
require around 3 million tons of oil every year to satisfy both military and civilian demand.
Wars are won as much by resources as by battles. Without oil, steel, coal, or food, major conflicts
can’t be sustained for long. That’s why today, countries still fight over resources even if
they don’t always admit it. Hitler was no different.
In the Atlantic, the machines the British leader, Winston Churchill, said he feared
most — the dreaded U-boats — ran on diesel fuel. Beneath the waves they switched to electric motors
powered by batteries, but they could only be recharged by diesel engines on the surface.
During the Battle of Britain, Germany committed around 2,500 bombers and 1,500 fighters. Every
aircraft depended on high-octane aviation fuel that could only be made with coal.
Britain actually had an edge on Germany because its Mark II Spitfires. The new “work-horses”,
the Hurricanes, ran on 100-octane aviation fuel imported from the US,
which was a more high-performance fuel than Germany’s synthetic oil.
Britain's fighters flew on American oil. Germany’s effectively flew on coal.
Then there were Germany's coal-hungry armored forces.
During the war the country produced between 26,000 and 45,000 tanks, along with hundreds
of thousands of trucks, half-tracks, motorcycles and other military vehicles. Railways carried much
of the army's supplies using coal-fired steam locomotives. But once soldiers,
fuel and ammunition left the railway, they depended on petrol and diesel to reach the front.
Even building those machines required vast quantities of petroleum products,
from lubricants and hydraulic fluids to synthetic rubber and industrial chemicals.
But for much of the war, Germany could meet the demand. It really was self-sufficient.
Tthen it all went wrong. Self-sufficiency came vulnerability.
In April 1944, Germany’s synthetic plants produced around 316,000 tons of fuel. It
was enough to keep the system functioning. Then the Allied oil offensive kicked off.
By June, production had fallen to around 107,000 tons. By September, it was down to just 17,000.
The figures varied from month to month as damaged plants were repaired and bombed again. But the
overall outlook was grim. Germany’s artificial oil industry was being systematically dismantled.
Albert Speer pleaded for more fighters and anti-aircraft guns to protect the plants.
Without them, Germany could still build tanks and aircraft, but if there wasn’t enough fuel,
then the shiny new vehicles were useless. Of course, this collapsing fuel supply wasn’t
the only reason the war had become unwinnable. Bad news was everywhere for the Nazis in ‘44.
German armies were retreating in the Soviet Union. The Western Allies had established
themselves in France. Germany’s cities and industries were being hammered from the air.
That’s why a group of senior officers and civilian conspirators decided that
Hitler was leading the country towards total destruction. The man was detached from reality,
and stubborn. He was obsessed with destiny, but often overlooked the hard facts.
Some of those conspirators had opposed him for years. Some were against the
horrific mass killings of Jews, Slavs, and civilians. Now time was running out.
Germany was on the brink. So, on July 20th, 1944, they did the previously unthinkable.
They tried to assassinate him. They came close, too. But Hitler
survived. Many of the conspirators were soon staring down the barrels of a firing squad.
Their attempt might have failed, but their assessment of Germany’s position was spot on.
6 months later, the Reich lost another foundation of its remaining power.
On January 12th, 1945, the Red Army launched the Vistula–Oder Offensive. Soviet forces tore
through the German front and advanced hundreds of miles in a matter of weeks. Just one week later,
Marshal Ivan Konev’s 1st Ukrainian Front reached the approaches to Upper Silesia, one of Germany’s
most important coal-mining and industrial regions. Given the importance of the region,
the Germans had prepared defensive positions and committed substantial forces to protecting
it. The mines were responsible for almost a quarter of Germany's annual output of coal,
81% of its zinc and 34% of its lead. The coke works, steel mills and metal-processing plants
were some of the last major industrial assets feeding Germany’s collapsing war economy.
Losing them would deprive the Reich not only of valuable resources, but the factories that turned
those resources into weapons. All of it was lost.
The Germans didn’t even manage to complete their scorched Earth policy
and blow up all the facilities. It was also bad news for the
Germans who lived in that region. Polish sources state that since the
Soviets considered the region German, not Polish, this wasn’t liberation. In Miechowice, a district
of Bytom, the Soviets massacred about 380 people. Looting, sexual violence, deportations and more
killings followed in other German areas. It was a brutal advance.
Yet it was here, in Upper Silesia, that the Red Army reached Auschwitz. The SS had tried to erase
the evidence by evacuating tens of thousands of prisoners and destroying parts of the camp. Even
so, the Soviets found gas chambers and crematoria, warehouses filled with victims' belongings, and
thousands of prisoners so emaciated they looked like the living dead. One of them was Primo Levi,
too ill to be evacuated. He would go on to tell the world what had happened there.
In March, Konev launched a separate Upper Silesian Offensive involving more than
400,000 Soviet troops. By the end of month, Germany had lost almost all practical access
to the region whose coal and metals had helped sustain its war machine.
Poland had oil reserves, too. At the start of the war,
it was producing about 10,500 barrels a day. Because the Soviets had split Poland with
Germany, Germany would only gain about 3,000 barrels after it took control of the wells.
It wasn’t much compared with the oil of Romania or the Caucasus, but every barrel mattered in a
total war. As the Red Army advanced westward in 1945, Germany lost those fields as well.
As one vital industrial center after another was left in flames or taken whole,
Germany had another problem. A serious tank problem.
Germany had created one of the most formidable killing machines in the
Panther. It was a machine that made Hitler proud. Unfortunately, it arrived just as Germany was
beginning to lose the fuel needed to run it. After rolling off the production line in 1943,
the Panther made its combat debut at the Battle of Kursk. Around 200 were committed to the offensive,
reportedly accounting for about 10% percent of Germany's armored force taking part.
Often described as the largest tank battle in history, Kursk saw around 2.8 million soldiers
and thousands of tanks thrown into combat. Germany committed 2,500 to 3,000, about 70% of its total
usable arsenal. That required a lot of fuel. Hitler desperately needed a victory. Not just to
regain the initiative, but to convince the public, and maybe himself, the war was still winnable.
The Panther fought alongside the fearsome Tiger and the Panzer IV, still the backbone of Germany's
armored forces. Waiting for them was the Soviet workhorse, the T-34. On paper, the Panther was
the superior fighting machine to them all. In reality, there was one really big problem.
It didn’t work. They kept breaking down.
The engines overheated. Bearings failed. Transmissions gave out. Fuel and oil leaks
sometimes sparked fires in the engine compartment, turning the tank into a death trap for its crew.
But when they did work, they were devastating. Some accounts credit the Panthers with destroying
hundreds of Soviet tanks during the battle while suffering comparatively few losses
in direct tank-versus-tank combat. But the Panthers greatest enemy was itself.
More were lost to mechanical failure than to Soviet fire. They were recalled but the
issues remained in one form or another. And again, there was an issue with fuel.
In his memoir, Colonel Helmut Ritgen of the Panzer Lehr Division explained that quote,
“during the war, we actually used every free minute of the day to train the men.”
But when the men were training for Kursk, known as Operation Citadel,
they “were forbidden to exercise” with their tanks because there wasn’t enough fuel.
German documents show that on July 5th, Operation Citadel had 184 Panthers in operation. Four
days later, there were only 10 remaining. 25 Panthers had been lost as total write-offs
and 100 were in desperate need of repair either through hits or mechanical failures.
It wasn’t just the Panthers that suffered. Research shows that out of nearly 1,700
Tiger I and Tiger II losses, only 40% were listed as combat losses.
Fuel shortages made everything worse, but they were only one part of the collapse.
Many of the tanks were just left there, in the mud. Crews abandoned them or placed demolition
charges inside the fighting compartment so that they couldn’t be captured intact.
Modern reports say the Tiger I might have taken 200,000 man-hours to build
and cost in the region of $100,000, maybe more. That’s almost $2 million today,
and the Tiger II was almost 3 times as much. The Panther might have taken 93,600 man-hours
to build and cost less than half of the Tiger I. That was good for the Germans, but
all those dumped in the mud had taken an enormous investment of steel, labour and scarce resources.
Germany wasn’t in a financial position to lose these machines. It needed every last penny it
could muster. It was busy making one of the most technologically advanced weapons of the century.
A weapon so advanced in fact that the Allies would not quite believe what they were seeing.
Soon, intel reached England that the Germans had a high-powered rocket that could reach England
when fired from Germany. Lord Cherwell, the chief scientific advisor to Winston Churchill during
the war, said something like, “Balderdash.” Such a thing is impossible, he confidently
remarked. He was wrong.
At about 7pm on Friday 8th September 1944, after there was a massive explosion that tore
through Staveley Road in Chiswick, London. The casualties included a toddler, an elderly lady
and a soldier from the Royal Engineers. The public were left wondering what had hit them.
British people had already watched in fear as Doodlebugs had flown in the sky
above their heads and landed unpredictably. About 10,000 of them were fired at England.
2,419 landed in London, killing about 6,1200 people and injuring 18,000 more.
Some made it to Greater Manchester and Yorkshire, the worst attack in the north
hitting Abbey Hills Road in Oldham, killing 27 people and injuring 49. People just never
knew where they would land. As a woman in Oldham said, “We heard the flying bomb going round and
round. Everything went quiet for a short time and then came the shattering bang.”
These things were absolutely terrifying, like nothing the English public had
experienced. Thankfully, many were intercepted or landed harmlessly where people didn’t live.
Guided only by a pre-set compass, odometer, and a fixed amount of fuel,
the Nazis could initially target only an area about 19 miles (31 km) across, later improving
the accuracy to around 7 miles (11km). The Brits called them Doodlebugs,
but their official name was the V-1. But whatever had made that crater in Chiswick
was an entirely different beast. It didn’t buzz in the sky. It didn’t just drop. It was a ghost.
Not long after the Chiswick attack, about 25 miles (40 km) away, another blast
seemingly came out of nowhere and reduced buildings to rubble in seconds. Soon after,
residents were looking into a giant crater. What kind of weapon could do that?
Nothing the public had ever heard of, that was for sure. The British government, not wanting to cause
panic, made up a story of a gas mains explosion. The people weren’t buying it.
Belgians were just as shocked when the same type of weapon hit a Rex Cinema in Antwerp on
December 16th, 1944. 567 people were killed: Belgian civilians and 296 Allied soldiers
from Britain, the US, Poland, and Canada. The Nazis might have been losing the war,
but they were about to rain vengeance down on London. And it was all thanks to the brilliant
mind of a German aerospace engineer, a dedicated Nazi party member with a touch of genius.
Wernher von Braun. He would become one of the most controversial
figures of the 20th century. Controversial, because he would become a future hero of NASA,
the “father of the American lunar program”, yet he’d also been an SS officer. A man whose
Nazi past and -- some say -- war crimes, were downplayed after the war because he was useful.
His V-2 rockets were built at the underground Mittelwerk factory by concentration camp
prisoners from nearby Mittelbau-Dora. Tens of thousands of slave laborers endured starvation,
beatings, exhaustion, and sometimes death. Highly-classified documents would show
how von Braun had ordered more of them. The deaths didn’t matter to the Germans.
They just needed manpower. What mattered more was that
the Nazis had technology that was maybe a decade or more ahead of Allied military science. British
and American officers were desperately trying to understand German military technology. And
in 1944, they found the Holy Grail at a secret site in the Coesfeld forest.
A full V-2 rocket with a 2,000-pound warhead in all its terrifying glory.
They’d already studied the weapon as much as possible. They’d captured components and had
intelligence, but this was the first time they got to see one in its perfect form.
It was like finding a miracle. They were virtually unstoppable.
Britain’s greatest fear was that Germany would attach chemical or biological weapons to them and
launch them at densely-populated areas in England. If that happened the damage would be incalculable.
The Nazis ran gas chambers where they murdered millions, but Hitler was never on-board with
chemical or biological weapons warfare. Even if he had been, he knew the Allies had vast chemical
and biological arsenals of their own and the last thing he needed was a massive counter-strike as
Germany already lay in flames. Such a retaliation in any form his country would not survive.
As great as the V-2s were, Germany could not win the war with them.
Still, they had about 6,000 that neither the British nor the Americans nor the
Russians could do anything to stop. A thousand pounds of warhead traveling at almost 3,600
mph (5,793 km/h) that could reach the edge of space. It was a major feat of scientific
endeavor that after the war, the Americans and Soviets would be desperate to replicate.
The Germans fired close to 1,409 at London and another 1,700 at Antwerp. So why didn't they
launch tens of thousands more? Especially as Germany was already losing the war.
First, the V-2 lacked a sophisticated guidance system. It could be aimed at a city,
but not at a specific building like the House of Commons or Winston Churchill's
residence. Early in the campaign, missiles often landed 6–12 miles (10–20 km) from their intended
target. Improvements to the guidance system later reduced that to around 3 miles (5 km).
It was a weapon of terror rather than precision. British post-war studies found that around 12%
landed harmlessly in the sea or remote countryside. Many never reached the
launch pad at all because they were rejected as defective or unstable.
The V-2 was an engineering marvel but a logistical nightmare. Each rocket demanded
enormous quantities of fuel, liquid oxygen, precision components and skilled labor. At a
time when Germany could barely keep its tanks moving and aircraft in the air,
producing enough V-2s to alter the course of the war was barely even conceivable.
And on top of that, they were expensive. Very expensive.
The Germans spent about $2 billion on them in 1944. That’s about $35 billion to $40 billion
today, a similar cost to the Manhattan Project. Each one in today’s money might have cost
$4.4 million, about 20 times more than the V-1 but not worth it considering the damage they caused.
The Germans also needed 20,000 slave laborers to build them, some who’d been executed for laziness
in what was brutal around-the-clock labor. 12,000 died in total, more than four times more people
than were killed in V-2 attacks on London. They didn’t run on gasoline but it took
coal and synthetic oil to power much of the industrial process that went into production.
They were greedy, too. The fuel was a mixture of 75%
ethyl alcohol (ethanol) and 25% water, mixed with liquid oxygen. That alcohol came from potatoes,
30 tons or thereabouts for just one launch. Researchers have said the V-2 program devoured
about one-third of Germany's entire industrial alcohol production. That was during a time when
soldiers on the battlefield needed feeding, when civilians were going hungry and when
prisoners were being executed because they no longer had the calories to render them useful.
The V-2 was a marvel. But in 1944, German wonder weapons were about to
be joined by technology from the Dark Ages. Germany liked to present itself as the army
of the future -- fast, mechanized and unstoppable. The blitzkrieg across Europe at the start of the
war was ample proof they weren’t overestimating themselves. They were powered by superior weapons
and methamphetamines that gave German soldiers that extra edge. Poland's ambassador to Britain,
Count Edward Bernard Raczyński, saw the writing on the wall. He described Poland’s
military situation as “hopeless” when German tanks and infantry poured across the border.
The devastation of those machines with men who barely seemed to sleep was beyond
anything ever seen. As the Polish First World War veteran Władysław Anders later
said after witnessing the fighting, “The nature of the new war was already clear.”
Nowhere did it seem more obvious than at the Battle of Krojanty.
Polish cavalry charged a surprised German infantry battalion, scattering the soldiers. Moments later,
German armored vehicles emerged from the trees and forced the cavalry into retreat, horsemen and
horses alike falling under machine-gun fire. Reports soon spread that the Polish cavalry
had charged German tanks, their lances against steel armor. The story wasn't true,
but it proved useful propaganda. For the Germans, it portrayed the Poles as
hopelessly outdated. For many Poles, it became a symbol of courage against impossible odds.
For everyone, it was a statement. The new versus the old.
What the newspapers and propaganda left out was that horses weren't obsolete,
far from it. In fact, they remained absolutely vital to every major army in the war.
During the 6 years of fighting, Germany relied on about 2.75 million horses, second
only to the Soviet Union, which used around 3.5 million. Tanks may have spearheaded the advance,
but horses hauled the food, ammunition, artillery and supplies that kept entire
armies on the move. On muddy roads, through forests and across terrain where vehicles
bogged down or broke apart, a horse was often far more dependable than a fuel-hungry truck.
They were fairly cheap, too. Their fuel was nature: grass and grain.
The problem, of course, is they didn’t fire weapons. They also needed tending
to. Bullets didn’t bounce off their skin and loud noises tended to spook them. So,
they weren’t always good in the thick of the fighting, but in the background,
they were excellent additions to the army. At various points throughout the war,
Germany’s horses pulled between 50% and 70% of Wehrmacht’s military supplies. During the entirety
of Operation Barbarossa, close to 200,000 horses didn’t make it out alive. They died from wounds,
starvation or exposure. But without them Germany’s
offensive hesitated or came to a stop. That didn't usually make it into Nazi propaganda
news reels. Hitler didn’t want his people seeing German officers on horseback. Animal power wasn’t
good for morale. Tiger tanks and flying aces were. But the fact was, without horses, the machines,
and the humans, ceased to function. That didn't mean they weren't a logistical
problem. Each horse consumed about 20 pounds (9 kg) of hay and oats a day. For a single division,
that meant hauling roughly 30 tons of fodder every day, 9 tons more than the food for the
men. In fact, the horses ate so much that their fodder outweighed the soldiers'
rations by 275%. They even exceeded the fuel needed for the division's vehicles by 165%.
The problem was bulk. And that bulk had to travel to the battlefield on ships and in vehicles. So,
while gasoline was a problem, so was making sure horses had the energy to do the grunt work.
But whenever such logistical problems were raised with the boss, Hitler often brushed
them aside. He reportedly complained that officers who brought up the issue
“made everything too complicated.” Then when the oil started to go,
he suddenly found himself relying on these animals more than he’d ever imagined he would.
He was becoming desperate. Every cow, every hungry horse, was proof.
And he was about to scrape the bottom of the barrel.
The Soviets and Western Allies began to enter Germany from opposite directions. So,
Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels appealed to his people in his infamous “Werewolf Broadcast”
to form an underground resistance. Like guerrillas, they were to assassinate
occupation officials, sabotage railways and communications, destroy supplies and wreak
havoc wherever the foreign occupiers settled. “We Werewolves,” he barked in one broadcast,
“consider it our supreme duty to kill, to kill and to kill – employing every cunning and wile
in the darkness of night, crawling, groping through towns and villages like wolves.”
In reality, very few Germans wanted to become terrorists. Beyond a handful of assassinations and
isolated acts of sabotage, the Werwolf campaign amounted to not much more than poetic bluster.
But Allied radio didn’t think so. It still warned its soldiers that every German civilian could be
a potential killer, a wolf in sheep’s clothing. “Every friendly German civilian is a disguised
soldier of hate,” one broadcast blared. “Their hatred and their anger ... are deeply buried in
their blood. A smile is their weapon by which to disarm you ... In heart,
body and spirit every German is Hitler.” That was far from the truth.
Most German civilians at that point just wanted the nightmare to end. When American or British
trucks of handsome soldiers passed, German women sometimes greeted them with smiles and
flowers. Yet fear of hidden resistance made many Allied soldiers deeply suspicious. That
was one of the reasons for massacres and the suffering German women experienced. Meanwhile,
in the east, the advancing Red Army unleashed a wave of extreme violence.
But the broadcasts were right about one thing. The Allies did have a reason to be suspicious.
Many Germans had taken up arms because they believed they were fighting for their country's
survival. Often, they were little more than boys, their helmets too big for their heads,
usually cut down with heartbreaking ease when faced with fighting grown men.
These weren't the feared Werewolves, but the Volkssturm, a people's militia made up of men
aged 16 to 60 who weren't already serving in the armed forces. Often poorly equipped, they were
Germany's last desperate line of defense. For years, Nazi propaganda had warned that
defeat would bring Germany's destruction at the hands of Judeo-Bolshevism and what they
said was Jewish-controlled capitalism. Ever since Stalingrad and Goebbels' famous “Total
War” speech in 1943, Germans had been told that surrender meant complete annihilation.
These evil forces would take over all of Europe and end their way of life.
Whether Germans at home believed it is another matter. Some obviously did,
but some were sceptical. Badly trained, the ones that did fight could sometimes be seen riding
through streets full of rubble with anti-tank weapons fitted to the front of their bicycles.
The bicycle squadron. From V-2 weapons,
to Panther tanks, to horses, to the bicycle. Total War had become Desperate War.
But bicycles at least bypassed the logistical hurdles that had plagued
Germany in 1944. Unlike machines, they needed no coal or oil to move them. And unlike horses,
they didn’t require bales of hay or sacks of oats and they didn’t buck at the sound of explosion.
But they were effectively little use against Allied firepower. The Allies would destroy 3.6
million German homes. Between 350,000 and 600,000 civilians would be killed in Allied bombing
campaigns, and another 800,000 wounded. Teenage boys riding bicycles with rockets attached were
never going to prevent any of that from happening. Even so, Hitler had dreamed of raising 6 million
men, the number available if every eligible civilian joined the Volkssturm. In reality,
perhaps 600,000 to one million served. Some bullied reluctant neighbors into
joining. Others committed war crimes. But as a military force, they were little more than
a symbol of Germany's desperation. During the Battle of Berlin,
around 60,000 Volkssturm found themselves fighting as part of a hopeless defense
against an overwhelming Soviet force. It’s believed Hitler was furious in his
bunker when he heard many members chose to hide rather than take on the Russian Goliath. Cowards,
he called them. They should have been happy to die for the cause. That was the noble thing to do.
Of course, he’d never himself stared down the turret of a tank. Like all military
leaders on all sides, he sat safely far away from the bullets and bombs.
If modern historians are right, his order to encourage every last German to fight led to
the needless deaths of 1.23 million citizens. Some didn’t have a choice. They were sometimes
shot or hanged if they refused to fight. When the Soviets arrived, many were killed
or captured and sent to the gulags. Hundreds of thousands of them went East and never returned.
It wasn’t easy being German at the war’s end. It didn’t matter if you’d never supported Hitler,
or the war, or if you weren’t antisemitic. The biggest insult was, Hitler didn’t care
about what happened to them once he knew the war was lost.
On March 7th, Allied troops flooded over the Rhine and captured the Ludendorff Bridge.
The Nazi’s last major defensive barrier had been breached allowing Allied forces to pour
into Germany. Although German engineers tried to demolish the bridge, they failed before soldiers
of the U.S. 9th Armored Division seized it. Germany’s last offensive of the war,
Operation Spring Awakening in Hungary against the Red Army, was crushed nine days later.
It was over. Germany had fired its last shot.
And so had Adolf Hitler. On April 30th, deep inside his Berlin bunker,
with Red Army shells exploding above, Hitler ended his life. His new wife, Eva Braun, lay dead beside
him after biting into a cyanide capsule. Goebbels, Hitler’s faithful servant,
is believed to have heard the news and said, “For us, everything is lost now
and the only way out left for us is the one Hitler chose. I shall follow his example.”
And he did. On May 1st, he swallowed cyanide.
Goebbels was an intelligent man. A fanatical antisemite, certainly,
but also one of history's most effective propagandists. More than perhaps anyone else,
he helped convince millions of ordinary Germans to embrace Hitler's vision of a racially pure
empire stretching across mainland Europe. Before his death, he had already contemplated
how history might judge him. “We shall go down in history,” he said,
“either as the greatest statesmen of all time or as the greatest criminals.”
For Hitler, his people had failed him. They were simply not strong enough in the end to
carry out his orders and make Germany the greatest country that ever existed.
He didn’t care what would happen to them after he was gone.
On March 18th, his Minister of Armaments, Albert Speer, had sent him a memorandum in
which Speer had said Germany might have 4 to 8 weeks before it was overrun. Speer was not
a fanatic, or at least not in the same league as Hitler’s inner circle. He informed Hitler
that the least they could do now was try to ensure the survival of the German people.
But for Hitler, if the people were truly loyal, they’d have gone fighting as he’d asked.
On March 19th, Hitler issued a decree titled “Destructive Measures on Reich Territory.”
This is also sometimes called the “Scorched Earth Decree” or “Nero Decree,” after the
tyrannical Roman emperor who watched Rome burn as he, according to legend, played the fiddle.
Destroy everything, Hitler said: roads, bridges, railroads, transportation facilities,
communication lines, industrial and supply installations, public utilities,
and of course, the factories and mines that had made Germany such a formidable country. Nothing
was exempted. If it was valuable, useful, blow it up. His orders went straight to his most loyal
commanders, to the politicians and Nazi Party administrative officials he knew would understand
and adhere to the order without question. Speer, who would later spend 20 years in prison
for being a fulcrum of the Nazi military machine, was shocked. In a letter back to Hitler dated
March 29th, he called this an injustice to the German people, adding, “I therefore beg you not
to carry out a step so destructive of the nation.” If Germany's infrastructure was to be destroyed,
he later wrote, then “I am preparing to destroy the foundation of their lives.”
Speer later claimed he confronted Hitler in the bunker and persuaded him to abandon the
order. There were no witnesses. After the war, Speer worked hard to portray himself as the
“good Nazi”. A man who was repentant, ethical and willing to stand up to Hitler. Whether his
account is entirely truthful remains a matter of debate. If he had confronted the Fuhrer like that,
there’s a good chance he’d have been shot for insubordination.
Whatever the case, the Nero Decree was never fully carried out.
The scary fact was, it didn’t even need to be. Much of Germany was already destroyed.
There wasn’t much left to tear down in many of the major cities.
But the Nero Decree serves as a symbolic reminder of Hitler’s unwavering extremism, his complete
devotion to his poisonous ideals. He’d rather see his country burn, his people burn with it,
than save something for them after he was gone. At the stroke of midnight, on May 8th, 1945,
Germany formally capitulated. The war in Europe ended as Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel
signed the German Instrument of Surrender. Germans call it Zero Hour, the moment that
their country made a complete break from the vile radicalism of the Nazi Party.
But this was no time for a celebration. Around 5.3 million German servicemen had
been killed. In the immediate post-war years, there were only 60 to 70 men aged 20 to 40 for
every 100 women. Hundreds of thousands of German civilians had died in Allied bombing campaigns.
In the years that followed, another 500,000 to 2 million Germans would die from starvation,
disease or violence as Europe struggled through the aftermath of the war.
And if Nazism had been a malignant tumor, it had spread deep into German society. It wasn't just a
series of military campaigns. It was an ideology woven into marriage, family life, schools, sport,
art, film, the workplace. It was ingrained in the way children were taught to think and parents
believed they ought to raise them. Was May 8th really Zero Hour?
Could something that had spread so deeply really disappear with the stroke of a pen?
No. Zero Hour was to a
large extent a myth. A noble lie that was needed to give the people a sense of a new beginning.
The proof is in the data. The Nazis received 37.3% of
the vote in July 1932. It wasn’t a majority, but enough to become the largest party in a Germany
devastated by mass unemployment, political violence and economic collapse. Millions
turned to Hitler believing he could rescue a nation that seemed almost unsalvageable.
For many ordinary Germans, he delivered on his promise.
Massive public works, rearmament and military expansion drove unemployment down. Farmers and
industrial workers often found themselves better off. At the same time, Hitler's government blamed
Germany's problems on Jews, Marxists and other supposed enemies. Hatred became embedded into
the state's institutions and everyday life. Life didn’t improve for everyone and certainly
not the enemies of the Nazis whose lives were completely ruined. According to the British
historian Ian Kershaw, by the late 1930s the regime enjoyed broad public support, about 90%
in some way or other. How many Germans embraced the Nazis’ most extreme crimes -- pogroms,
forced labor, mass murder and total ideological control -- is impossible to know in a nation
pervaded by censorship and fear. But millions accepted, tolerated or benefited from the system
that made those crimes possible. So when Zero Hour came,
Hitler still had a lot of support. In 1946, when Germans already knew about
the Holocaust. A poll by the US Occupying Forces revealed that 25-30% of Germans still supported
the idea of National Socialism. A very unnerving 37% in another poll agreed that “the extermination
of the Jews and Poles and other non-Aryan races was necessary for the security of Germany.”
The “absolute break” from the Nazis at Zero Hour, the new beginning, was far from reality.
The regime had brainwashed a nation and for many people, accepting they’d been wrong
was an assault on their existence. It would take years of re-education, of occupation,
of denazification, for Germany to free itself from the cancer of the Nazis. In some cases,
all over Europe, this denazification process led to extrajudicial murders.
This alone tells us there was no happy and sudden break from Nazism.
And around 7.5 million Germans had been left homeless in a country of rubble. Millions faced
hunger as food shortages gripped the nation, and many died from disease and malnutrition
in the difficult years that followed. Crime flourished. Black markets became a way of life.
Women across occupied Germany also faced another terror during Zero Hour. They were assaulted by
soldiers from every occupying army. The worst atrocities occurred in the east under the Red
Army, but American, French and British troops also committed thousands of these assaults.
In total, between 1 million and 2 million German women and girls became victims. An
estimated 240,000 were killed in the process by troops from all occupying nations.
For countless Germans, the war did not end on May 8, it just took on a different form. It would be
an insult to call this time rebirth. But that’s what some German and western media called it -- a
“spiritual rebirth” and “radical new beginning.” It also didn’t feel like that for the many
millions of Germans who flooded into the country from previously occupied territories. Many found
hatred, resentment, discrimination and violence. Returning Jews who’d survived the holocaust were
sometimes referred to as “parasitic foreigners.” It was as if nothing had changed.
Those without money scavenged among the ruins for food and fuel. Returning soldiers wandered
bombed-out streets looking for work, some even finding themselves blamed by their wives for
losing the war. Children did the same. Reports described gangs of orphaned boys roaming the
rubble in search of anything they could eat, burn or sell. In one case, making a
home out of an abandoned public swimming pool. But brick by brick, the people re-built their
country as an Iron Curtain cut Europe in half. The Soviet Union became the new enemy of Britain and
the USA and its ally, West Germany. With West Germany now on side, rehabilitation was more
important than facing past atrocities. Western governments and media even occasionally downplayed
them in what could be said to have been omission propaganda or a case of selective amnesia.
As the years passed, Germans rarely talked about certain aspects of the war:
the horrors they’d witnessed, or in some cases, the horrors they’d perpetrated. The holocaust
became almost a taboo topic in some households. Many preferred to remember themselves as victims
rather than participants. Few spoke openly about jeering at Jewish neighbors as they
were driven from their home and taking over expropriated businesses. They forgot about
denouncing friends, colleagues and relatives to the authorities for failing to be “good”
Germans. Nazi indoctrination had even persuaded some children to inform on their own parents.
This would take a lifetime to rebuild but the scars never quite went away. The physical ruins
of Germany could be cleared in a few years. But the moral ruins remained scattered in the minds of
the people. It would take generations to root out the last remnants of Nazi ideology and to confront
what had happened between 1933 and 1945. But confront it they did, because those
who don’t reflect on history might be doomed to repeat it one day.
